rv.q: There was not a second during this transporting evening of being even slightly tempted to glance at one's watch or to remember one was in a theatre at all.
Ultimately 'Small Island' is a ferociously entertaining three hours of theatre, told with the sort of overwhelming resources only the National can marshal.
Small Island has found its ideal home. This feels like a landmark for the National (and a defining success for Rufus Norris's sometimes troubled regime).
The best thing about Rufus Norris's fluent production is a spectacular design by Katrina Lindsay.
In the end this is a passionate engagement with the past that's sure to resonate with audiences at a time when the very idea of Britain is under such fierce scrutiny.
Rather than turn Small Island into theatre, it merely sits Levy's story on a stage.
It is a shame then that – despite some excellent performances – Rufus Norris' production is so often tone-deaf.

Sweeping when needed but also touchingly intimate, the production deploys the full resources of the National...to tell a rending story of displacement that finds goodness where other such tales would merely come to grief.
This is a magnificent work of art, a moving and brilliantly detailed tapestry of England in the early post-war years.
This critic urges you to attend a performance.
Small Island is a sweeping drama of a period in Britain's history that it should really be ashamed of and it's superbly directed by Rufus Norris.
On the other hand, it's hard to deny that the production is big, bold and spectacular, as well as accessible, relevant and fulsomely entertaining.

cn.t: Helen Edmundson's adaptation of Andrea Levy's Windrush novel earns strong praise as confident, emotionally resonant theater that brings vital social history to vivid life, despite its lengthy runtime.
